guidance: Uneven runs usually mean uneven fingers — the fourth and fifth doing less work than the rest, which is exactly the weakness Hanon wrote Part 1 to attack. Play the first exercises slowly, lifting each finger with the same precision and drawing the same volume from every note, so no finger hides inside the pattern. Evenness at a slow tempo is the whole exercise; speed without it just rehearses the lump.

Czerny's School of Velocity is built on the rule that speed is earned, never grabbed: begin each study far below the target tempo with a strict metronome and perfect evenness, and raise the click one notch only when the current tempo feels effortless. If a passage falls apart when you push it, you skipped notches — drop back to the last tempo that was clean and climb again. The metronome is the honest witness here.

topic: Hands separately, then together in small sections
guidance: Czerny's beginner method takes coordination apart before putting it together: practice each hand alone until it is genuinely secure — not merely survivable — then join the hands in small sections, a phrase or less at a time. When hands-together playing breaks down, the honest move is backward: return to separate hands on just the failing bars, rebuild each part, and rejoin them slowly. Coordination is assembled, not willed.
